--- title: "Capacity Expansion" subtitle: "Lecture 16" author: "Vivek Srikrishnan" course: "BEE 4750" institution: "Cornell University" date: "November 2, 2026" format: revealjs: slide-number: c/t show-slide-number: all center-title-slide: true width: 1280 height: 720 transition: none toc: true toc-depth: 1 toc-title: "Overview" history: false link-external-newwindow: true theme: ../sass/slides.scss template-partials: - title-slide.html menu: numbers: true html-math-method: mathjax include-in-header: mathjax-config.html date-format: long email-obfuscation: javascript chalkboard: theme: whiteboard buttons: true controls: true engine: julia julia: exeflags: ["+1.11.5"] execute: freeze: auto daemon: 600 --- # Review and Questions ## Last Class: Economic Dispatch - Dispatch runs the plants we **already have** at least cost: the merit order, bent by minimum outputs and ramping. - **The price of electricity is the demand constraint's shadow price**: the cost of the plant that would serve the next MWh (\$38/MWh at 2200 MW). Today: deciding what to **build**. ::: {.notes} Budget a couple of minutes to re-sync after last week. The Wednesday dispatch lecture was taught by a substitute; ask whether anything from it was unclear, especially the sign of the shadow price (relaxing demand means serving one less MWh, so JuMP reports a negative number). ::: ## Questions? :::: {.columns .center} ::: {.column width="40%"} ![](figures/vsrikrish-poll.png){fig-alt="Poll Everywhere QR Code" fig-align="center" width="100%"} ::: ::: {.column width=60%} **Text**: VSRIKRISH to 22333 **URL**: [https://pollev.com/vsrikrish](https://pollev.com/vsrikrish)

[See Results](https://www.polleverywhere.com/multiple_choice_polls/qKeig0hHShZYHAOmvZtZm?preview=true&controls=none){preview-link="true"} ::: :::: # The Capacity Expansion Problem ## Capacity Expansion **Capacity expansion**: which generating resources to build, and how much, to meet future demand (*load*). - Typical objective: minimize cost. - Other goals may enter as constraints: reducing CO~2~ emissions, fuel diversity, reliability. We'll look at a **greenfield** problem (no existing plants), not a **brownfield** one (adding to an existing fleet). ::: {.notes} This sits at the long end of the decision time scales from last week: years, not hours. The dispatch decision is nested inside it: whatever we build has to be run every hour, and the running costs are part of the case for building it. Most real planning is brownfield. Mini-Project 2's final part is one: New York's 2013 fleet is already there, and the plan adds to it. ::: ## Plant Types - natural gas: **combined cycle** (CCGT) or **combustion turbines** (CT); - coal and nuclear; - renewables: wind, solar, hydro, geothermal. They differ in **what they cost to build** and **what they cost to run**, and the model has to weigh one against the other. ::: {.notes} Preview the result: cheap-to-build plants that are expensive to run (CTs) suit loads that occur only a few hours a year; expensive-to-build plants that are cheap to run suit loads that are there all year. The rest of the lecture makes that precise. ::: # Formulating the Problem ## Data: Generators and Demand ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} gens = DataFrame(CSV.File("data/capacity_expansion/generators.csv")) n_types = nrow(gens) - 2 # leave out wind and solar for now println("| Generator | Fixed cost (\\\$/MW-yr) | Variable cost (\\\$/MWh) |") println("|:--|--:|--:|") for g in 1:n_types println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) | $(commas(gens[g, :FixedCost])) | $(gens[g, :VarCost]) |") end ``` | Generator | Fixed cost (\$/MW-yr) | Variable cost (\$/MWh) | |:--|--:|--:| | Nuclear | 790,000 | 8 | | Coal | 220,000 | 21 | | NG CCGT | 82,000 | 25 | | NG CT | 65,000 | 35 | Demand: NYISO Zone C, every hour of 2020 (peak 2,781 MW). ::: {.notes} Fixed costs are annualized: the cost of building one MW of capacity, spread over the plant's life, per year. Variable costs are per MWh generated. Nuclear is very expensive to build and cheap to run; combustion turbines are the reverse. Wind and solar return later. ::: ## Load Duration Curve ::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} sorted_demand = sort(demand, rev=true) p_ldc = plot(1:n_hours, sorted_demand, color=:black, xlabel="Hours of the year with at least this load", ylabel="Load [MW]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 3000)) plot!(p_ldc, size=(1200, 360), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: The year's hourly loads, sorted from highest to lowest, show **how many hours** each load level is reached. ::: {.notes} The chronological demand curve (one point per hour through the year) makes it hard to see how often each level occurs. Sorting turns it into a load duration curve: read any point as "the load is at least this high for this many hours". The top few hundred MW are needed only a handful of hours a year; the bottom 1,000 MW or so are needed every hour. ::: ## Decision Variables What are our variables? ::: {.fragment .fade-in} | Variable | Meaning | |:--:|:-------------------| | $x_g$ | installed capacity (MW) of generator type $g \in \mathcal{G}$ | | $y_{g,t}$ | production (MWh) of type $g$ in hour $t \in \mathcal{T}$ | | $NSE_t$ | non-served energy (MWh) in hour $t$ | ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Must we meet the very highest hour? Price **non-served energy** at \$9,000/MWh and let the model decide. ::: ::: {.notes} Two kinds of decisions: how much to build (x, one per technology) and how to run it each hour (y, one per technology per hour). Non-served energy is load we choose not to serve; its cost stands in for the damage of a shortfall. 9,000 dollars per MWh is in the range of real market price caps. ::: ## The Formulation Write the objective and constraints. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} ::: {.small-math} $$ \begin{aligned} \min_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{NSE}} \quad & \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \text{FixedCost}_g \, x_g + \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} \text{VarCost}_g \, y_{g,t} \\ & \quad + \sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}} \text{NSECost} \, NSE_t \\[0.3em] \text{subject to:} \quad & \sum_{g \in \mathcal{G}} y_{g,t} + NSE_t \geq d_t \qquad \forall t \in \mathcal{T} \\[0.3em] & y_{g,t} \leq x_g \qquad \forall g \in \mathcal{G}, t \in \mathcal{T} \\[0.3em] & x_g, \, y_{g,t}, \, NSE_t \geq 0 \end{aligned} $$ ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Board item; the fragment is the answer. Build the objective in two pieces: investment (fixed cost times capacity) and operation (variable cost times generation, plus the penalty on unserved energy). Constraints: each hour, generation plus unserved energy covers demand; no plant produces more than its installed capacity; everything is non-negative. Ask: is this an LP? Yes: it's linear in every variable, capacity is divisible (we model total MW, not individual units), and demand is treated as known. Each of those three is an assumption we'll revisit: discrete units (Wednesday), uncertainty (in two weeks). ::: # Solving and Reading the Answer ## Implementation in `JuMP` ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false" code-line-numbers="|1|3-7|8-9|10-11|12"} NSECost = 9000 gencap = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) @variables(gencap, begin x[g in 1:n_types] >= 0 # capacity [MW] y[g in 1:n_types, t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # generation [MWh] NSE[t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # non-served energy [MWh] end) @objective(gencap, Min, sum(gens[g, :FixedCost] * x[g] for g in 1:n_types) + sum(gens[g, :VarCost] * y[g, t] for g in 1:n_types, t in 1:n_hours) + NSECost * sum(NSE)) @constraint(gencap, load[t in 1:n_hours], sum(y[:, t]) + NSE[t] >= demand[t]) @constraint(gencap, availability[g in 1:n_types, t in 1:n_hours], y[g, t] <= x[g]) set_silent(gencap); optimize!(gencap) ``` ::: ::: {.notes} 8,784 hours times four technologies is about 35,000 generation variables; HiGHS solves it in a few seconds. Name the load and availability constraints so we can ask for their shadow prices later. ::: ## Results ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} capacity = value.(x) generation = [sum(value.(y[g, :])) for g in 1:n_types] unserved = value.(NSE) nse_hours = count(unserved .> 1e-6) # Cost and emissions of this plan, to compare with the plans that follow thermal_cost = objective_value(gencap) # [$/yr] thermal_emissions = sum(gens[g, :Emissions] * generation[g] for g in 1:n_types) # [t CO₂/yr] # One decimal place, and plain 0 rather than -0.0 for technologies that aren't built function share(v) rounded_v = round(v; digits=1) if rounded_v == 0 return "0" end return string(rounded_v) end println("| Resource | Installed (MW) | % of peak | % of energy |") println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|") for g in 1:n_types println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) | $(commas(capacity[g])) | $(share(100 * capacity[g] / peak_demand)) | ", "$(share(100 * generation[g] / sum(demand))) |") end ``` | Resource | Installed (MW) | % of peak | % of energy | |:--|--:|--:|--:| | Nuclear | 0 | 0 | 0 | | Coal | 0 | 0 | 0 | | NG CCGT | 2,017 | 72.5 | 98.1 | | NG CT | 733 | 26.4 | 1.9 | Up to **31 MW** goes unserved, in **7 hours** of the year. ::: {.notes} No nuclear and no coal: neither is worth building at these costs. Combined-cycle gas carries almost all of the energy; combustion turbines provide about a quarter of the capacity but only about 2% of the energy: they're for the peaks. And there is some unserved energy, despite the 9,000 dollar penalty: 94 MWh over 7 hours. The next slides explain all three facts from the cost data alone. The total cost is \$603M a year. ::: ## When Do Generators Run? ::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # The week around the year's peak hour peak_hour = argmax(demand) week = max(1, peak_hour - 84):min(n_hours, peak_hour + 83) run_by_type = zeros(length(week), n_types + 1) for g in 1:n_types run_by_type[:, g] = value.(y[g, week]) end run_by_type[:, end] = unserved[week] areaplot(1:length(week), run_by_type, label=permutedims([gens[1:n_types, :Plant]; "Unserved"]), color=permutedims([cb_purple, :gray40, cb_orange, cb_vermillion, :black]), xlabel="Hour of the peak week", ylabel="Generation [MW]", legend=:outerright, size=(1200, 440), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} One week, centred on the year's peak hour (a full year of hours is unreadable). The CCGTs run nearly all the time; the CTs come on only for the daily peaks; and in the highest hour or two, a thin sliver of demand goes unserved. ::: ## Screening Curves ::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Annual cost of one MW of each technology, as a function of how many hours it runs hours_run = 0:n_hours annual_cost = zeros(length(hours_run), n_types + 1) for g in 1:n_types annual_cost[:, g] = gens[g, :FixedCost] .+ gens[g, :VarCost] .* hours_run end annual_cost[:, end] = NSECost .* hours_run # not serving: no build cost ct_vs_ccgt = (gens[3, :FixedCost] - gens[4, :FixedCost]) / (gens[4, :VarCost] - gens[3, :VarCost]) nse_vs_ct = gens[4, :FixedCost] / (NSECost - gens[4, :VarCost]) p_screen = plot(xlabel="Hours run per year", ylabel="Cost per MW [\$1000/yr]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 900), legend=:outerright) for (j, (name, color, style)) in enumerate(zip([gens[1:n_types, :Plant]; "Unserved"], [cb_purple, :gray40, cb_orange, cb_vermillion, :black], [:solid, :dash, :solid, :dashdot, :dot])) plot!(p_screen, hours_run, annual_cost[:, j] ./ 1000, color=color, linestyle=style, label=name) end vline!(p_screen, [ct_vs_ccgt], color=:black, linewidth=1, linestyle=:dash, label=false) annotate!(p_screen, ct_vs_ccgt + 150, 680, text("$(commas(ct_vs_ccgt)) h", 16, :left, plot_font)) plot!(p_screen, size=(1200, 440), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.notes} Each line is what one MW of a technology costs per year if it runs for a given number of hours: fixed cost at zero hours, rising at the variable cost. The cheapest technology for a load that lasts h hours is the lowest line at h. Nuclear and coal are never lowest within a year. CTs are cheapest below the crossover with CCGT; CCGTs above. Unserved energy (the dotted line, steepest of all) is cheapest only for loads that last a few hours: its crossover with CTs is too close to zero to see at this scale. ::: ## Where the Lines Cross Find the crossovers: below how many hours a year is a CT cheaper than a CCGT? Not serving cheaper than a CT? ::: {.fragment .fade-in} $$ \begin{aligned} \text{CT vs. CCGT:} \quad & 65{,}000 + 35h = 82{,}000 + 25h \\ \text{Unserved vs. CT:} \quad & 9{,}000h = 65{,}000 + 35h \end{aligned} $$ A CT is cheaper below **1,700 hours**; not serving is cheaper below **7\.25 hours**. ::: ::: {.notes} Board item; the fragment is the answer. Set the two annual costs equal and solve. CCGT costs 17,000 dollars a year more to build and 10 dollars per MWh less to run, so it pays back after 1,700 hours. A CT costs 65,000 dollars a year to build; not serving costs 8,965 dollars more per MWh than running the CT, so a CT pays for itself only if it would run more than about seven hours a year. Coal never beats CCGT: the crossover is at 34,500 hours, longer than a year. Nuclear's crossover with CCGT is at about 41,600 hours. ::: ## Reading the Build Off the Curve ::: {#20 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} ccgt_level = sorted_demand[ceil(Int, ct_vs_ccgt)] ct_top = sorted_demand[ceil(Int, nse_vs_ct)] p_full = plot(1:n_hours, sorted_demand, color=:black, xlabel="Hours", ylabel="Load [MW]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 3000), title="Whole year") hline!(p_full, [ccgt_level], color=cb_orange, linestyle=:dash) vline!(p_full, [ct_vs_ccgt], color=:gray50, linewidth=1) annotate!(p_full, 2300, ccgt_level + 200, text("CCGT below $(commas(ccgt_level)) MW", 15, :left, plot_font)) p_top = plot(1:24, sorted_demand[1:24], color=:black, marker=:circle, xlabel="Hours", ylabel="Load [MW]", title="Top 24 hours", ylims=(2600, 2800)) hline!(p_top, [ct_top], color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dash) vline!(p_top, [nse_vs_ct], color=:gray50, linewidth=1) annotate!(p_top, 11, ct_top + 22, text("CT up to $(commas(ct_top)) MW", 15, :left, plot_font)) plot(p_full, p_top, layout=(1, 2), size=(1200, 350), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: CCGT **2,017 MW**, CT **733 MW**, **31 MW** unserved, which is exactly what the LP builds. ::: {.notes} Read the crossovers off the load duration curve. Load that lasts more than 1,700 hours is cheapest served by CCGT: that's the curve's height at 1,700 hours, 2,017 MW. Load lasting between about 7 and 1,700 hours is cheapest served by CTs: up to the curve's height at 8 hours. Load lasting fewer hours isn't worth building for at all. This reproduces the LP's build to the megawatt, and it answers why there's unserved energy despite the 9,000 dollar penalty: the last 31 MW are needed for only 7 hours a year, and building capacity for them would cost more than the penalty. The 7.25-hour threshold depends on the penalty: at 10,000 dollars per MWh it's 6.5 hours. ::: # Adding Renewables ## What Changes With Renewables? Wind and solar can't produce at full capacity every hour: their **capacity factor** $c_{g,t}$ depends on the weather. ::: {.fragment .fade-in} The capacity constraint changes from $$y_{g,t} \leq x_g \qquad \text{to} \qquad y_{g,t} \leq x_g \times c_{g,t}$$ ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} So a renewable's value depends on **when** it produces, and screening curves alone no longer give the answer. ::: ::: {.notes} For thermal plants, c is 1 in every hour. A MW of solar that produces at midday when load is low is worth less than one that produces at the evening peak. That's why the screening-curve shortcut breaks: the cost of a renewable MW depends on the hours it produces, not just on how many. The next slides add wind and solar to today's problem and work through what changes. ::: ## Where Capacity Factors Come From - Resource data: wind, sun, water or heat available each hour. - Often a **typical meteorological year (TMY)** or a few **actual meteorological years (AMY)**, sometimes only selected periods. - Both **underrepresent** variability, but keep the problem tractable. Always check what weather data a study used. Ours is for a **good wind and solar site**, not New York. ::: {.notes} A typical meteorological year stitches together typical months from many years, which smooths out the extremes: the windless week, the cloudy month. Planning for a typical year can under-build for the bad ones. That's a structural choice in the model, in the sense of October 7. Today's profiles are for a much better site than upstate New York, so the plan they give is for that kind of resource. It is not a forecast for New York. ::: ## Wind and Solar Capacity Factors ::: {#22 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} profiles = DataFrame(CSV.File("data/capacity_expansion/wind_solar_capacity_factors.csv")) # The profiles cover a 365-day year and 2020 has 366 days, so February 28 is used again for February 29 before_leap_day = 1:(59 * 24) feb28 = (58 * 24 + 1):(59 * 24) after_leap_day = (59 * 24 + 1):nrow(profiles) wind_cf = [profiles.Wind[before_leap_day]; profiles.Wind[feb28]; profiles.Wind[after_leap_day]] solar_cf = [profiles.Solar[before_leap_day]; profiles.Solar[feb28]; profiles.Solar[after_leap_day]] wind_average = sum(wind_cf) / n_hours solar_average = sum(solar_cf) / n_hours # Average capacity factor in each hour of the day n_days = div(n_hours, 24) wind_by_hour = zeros(24) solar_by_hour = zeros(24) for h in 1:24 wind_by_hour[h] = sum(wind_cf[h:24:end]) / n_days solar_by_hour[h] = sum(solar_cf[h:24:end]) / n_days end p_profiles = plot(1:24, wind_by_hour, color=cb_sky, label="wind", xlabel="Hour of the day", ylabel="Average capacity factor", ylims=(0, 1), xticks=0:6:24, legend=:topleft) plot!(p_profiles, 1:24, solar_by_hour, color=cb_orange, linestyle=:dash, label="solar") plot!(p_profiles, size=(1200, 350), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Over the year, wind averages **34%** and solar **35%**. ::: {.notes} The figure averages each hour of the day over the whole year. Solar produces only in daylight and peaks at midday. Wind is steadier across the day and a little stronger at night. The two annual averages are close, but the hours are very different, and that is what will matter. ::: ## Do Screening Curves Still Work? ::: {#24 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Wind and solar on the screening chart: a fixed cost each year, and nothing per MWh wind_row = n_types + 1 solar_row = n_types + 2 solar_vs_ct = (gens[solar_row, :FixedCost] - gens[4, :FixedCost]) / gens[4, :VarCost] wind_vs_ccgt = (gens[wind_row, :FixedCost] - gens[3, :FixedCost]) / gens[3, :VarCost] # What a MWh costs once the capacity factor is counted [$/MWh] wind_energy_cost = gens[wind_row, :FixedCost] / (wind_average * n_hours) solar_energy_cost = gens[solar_row, :FixedCost] / (solar_average * n_hours) p_renewable_screen = plot(xlabel="Hours run per year", ylabel="Cost per MW [\$1000/yr]", xlims=(0, n_hours), ylims=(0, 320), legend=:outerright) plot!(p_renewable_screen, hours_run, annual_cost[:, 3] ./ 1000, color=cb_orange, label="NG CCGT") plot!(p_renewable_screen, hours_run, annual_cost[:, 4] ./ 1000, color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dashdot, label="NG CT") hline!(p_renewable_screen, [gens[wind_row, :FixedCost] / 1000], color=cb_sky, linestyle=:dash, label="Wind") hline!(p_renewable_screen, [gens[solar_row, :FixedCost] / 1000], color=cb_green, linestyle=:dot, label="Solar") plot!(p_renewable_screen, size=(1200, 370), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} By the screening rule, solar serves every load over **143 hours** a year and no CCGT is built. What is missing? ::: ::: {.notes} Board item. Wind and solar cost the same each year however much they run, so their lines are flat. Solar's line is below CCGT's at every number of hours, and below CT's beyond 143 hours. Wind's is below CCGT's beyond 360 hours. Let the room say what is wrong before moving on. The chart assumes a plant can run in whichever hours it is needed. A MW of solar runs only when the sun is up: 35% of its capacity on average, mostly around midday, and never on request. ::: ## The Cost of a Solar MWh A MW of solar costs \$70,000 a year and averages 35% of its capacity. What does a MWh cost? ::: {.fragment .fade-in} - Solar: 70,000 ÷ (0\.346 × 8,784 h) = **\$23/MWh** - Wind: 91,000 ÷ (0\.342 × 8,784 h) = **\$30/MWh** - CCGT fuel: **\$25/MWh** ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} Solar's energy costs less than the gas it saves, so some is worth building. **How much** is a question for the LP. ::: ::: {.notes} Board item; the fragments carry the answer. Divide the annual cost of a MW by the MWh it actually produces. A CCGT that is already built saves \$25 of fuel for every MWh something else supplies. Solar's MWh costs less than that, so replacing gas energy with solar saves money. Wind's costs a little more on average, but wind can still pay in the hours when a CT at \$35 would otherwise run. Neither can be counted on in a given hour, so neither replaces the gas capacity itself. Comparing a new plant's cost per MWh with the fuel it would replace is the comparison to make whenever the capacity it competes with is needed anyway. ::: ## In `JuMP` ::: {#26 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Share of each type's capacity that is available each hour: all of it for the # thermal types, the capacity factor for wind and solar (the last two types) n_all = nrow(gens) available = ones(n_all, n_hours) available[wind_row, :] = wind_cf available[solar_row, :] = solar_cf # The least-cost plan for the listed plant types, with an optional cap on annual emissions [t CO₂] function solve_plan(types; cap=Inf, fixed_cost=gens.FixedCost) model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer) @variables(model, begin x[g in types] >= 0 # capacity [MW] y[g in types, t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # generation [MWh] nse[t in 1:n_hours] >= 0 # non-served energy [MWh] end) @expression(model, emitted, sum(gens[g, :Emissions] * y[g, t] for g in types, t in 1:n_hours)) @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed_cost[g] * x[g] for g in types) + sum(gens[g, :VarCost] * y[g, t] for g in types, t in 1:n_hours) + NSECost * sum(nse)) @constraint(model, [t in 1:n_hours], sum(y[g, t] for g in types) + nse[t] >= demand[t]) @constraint(model, [g in types, t in 1:n_hours], y[g, t] <= x[g] * available[g, t]) if isfinite(cap) @constraint(model, emissions_cap, emitted <= cap) end set_silent(model) optimize!(model) build = zeros(n_all) # capacity by type [MW]; zero for types left out hourly = zeros(n_all, n_hours) # generation by type and hour [MWh] energy = zeros(n_all) # generation by type over the year [MWh] for g in types build[g] = value(x[g]) for t in 1:n_hours hourly[g, t] = value(y[g, t]) end energy[g] = sum(hourly[g, :]) end carbon_price = 0 if isfinite(cap) carbon_price = shadow_price(emissions_cap) end return (types=types, build=build, hourly=hourly, energy=energy, unserved=value.(nse), cost=objective_value(model), emissions=value(emitted), carbon_price=carbon_price) end ``` ::: ```julia @constraint(model, [g in types, t in 1:n_hours], y[g, t] <= x[g] * available[g, t]) ``` Only the availability constraint changes: `available[g, t]` is 1 for the thermal types and the capacity factor for wind and solar. ::: {.notes} The folded cell holds the whole model as a function, so the same code can be solved for any set of plant types, with or without an emissions cap. Everything in it is the model from earlier except this one line. Writing the constraint with indexed sets keeps it one line however many technologies there are. ::: ## The Plan With Wind and Solar ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} with_renewables = solve_plan(1:n_all) # Totals of the whole-MW values the table shows, so the text and the table agree renewables_added = round(with_renewables.build[wind_row]) + round(with_renewables.build[solar_row]) gas_before = round(capacity[3]) + round(capacity[4]) gas_after = round(with_renewables.build[3]) + round(with_renewables.build[4]) # The same model at overnight costs with no tax credits (EIA: wind $153,000, solar $141,000 per MW-yr) no_credit_cost = copy(gens.FixedCost) no_credit_cost[wind_row] = 153000 no_credit_cost[solar_row] = 141000 no_credit = solve_plan(1:n_all; fixed_cost=no_credit_cost) println("::: {.small}\n") println("| | Thermal types only | With wind and solar |") println("|:--|--:|--:|") for g in 1:n_all if g <= n_types before = commas(capacity[g]) built_before = capacity[g] else before = "–" built_before = 0 end if built_before > 0.5 || with_renewables.build[g] > 0.5 println("| $(gens[g, :Plant]) (MW) | $(before) | $(commas(with_renewables.build[g])) |") end end println("| Cost (\\\$M/yr) | $(commas(thermal_cost / 1e6)) | $(commas(with_renewables.cost / 1e6)) |") println("| CO~2~ (kt/yr) | $(commas(thermal_emissions / 1000)) | $(commas(with_renewables.emissions / 1000)) |") println("\n:::") ``` ::: {.small} | | Thermal types only | With wind and solar | |:--|--:|--:| | NG CCGT (MW) | 2,017 | 1,574 | | NG CT (MW) | 733 | 726 | | Wind (MW) | – | 525 | | Solar (MW) | – | 1,506 | | Cost (\$M/yr) | 603 | 570 | | CO~2~ (kt/yr) | 6,679 | 4,055 | ::: Wind and solar add **2,031 MW**; gas falls by only **450 MW**. ::: {.notes} Three things change. Wind and solar are built: 2,031 MW between them. The gas plants run less: CCGTs supplied 98% of the energy before and 58% now, which is where the saving of \$33M a year and the 39% cut in emissions come from. And the gas capacity hardly changes, from 2,750 to 2,300 MW, because demand after dark still has to be met. Nuclear and coal are not built in either plan. This result depends on the costs. These wind and solar costs give energy at about \$30 and \$23 per MWh at this site, close to recent U.S. estimates that include tax credits. At overnight costs without credits (\$153,000 and \$141,000 per MW-year, from the Energy Information Administration's capital cost estimates), the same model builds 0 MW of wind and solar. ::: ## A Week With Wind and Solar ::: {#30 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} # The same peak week as before, under the plan with wind and solar built = findall(with_renewables.build .> 0.5) week_mix = zeros(length(week), length(built) + 1) for (j, g) in enumerate(built) week_mix[:, j] = with_renewables.hourly[g, week] end week_mix[:, end] = with_renewables.unserved[week] type_colors = [cb_purple, :gray40, cb_orange, cb_vermillion, cb_sky, cb_yellow] areaplot(1:length(week), week_mix, label=permutedims([gens[built, :Plant]; "Unserved"]), color=permutedims([type_colors[built]; :black]), xlabel="Hour of the peak week", ylabel="Generation [MW]", legend=:outerright, size=(1200, 350), left_margin=12mm) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: Gas still covers the evenings, so its capacity barely falls. ::: {.notes} The same week as the earlier figure. Solar fills the middle of each day and wind comes and goes. Every evening the gas plants climb back to nearly the output they had without wind and solar. This is last week's duck curve, seen from the planner's side: the capacity is still needed, but it runs fewer hours. ::: # Carbon Limits ## Capping Emissions ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} half_cap = 0.5 * thermal_emissions # [t CO₂/yr] capped_thermal = solve_plan(1:n_types; cap=half_cap) capped_all = solve_plan(1:n_all; cap=half_cap) # The next slide's title quotes this number @assert round(Int, -capped_thermal.carbon_price) == 148 # One table row for a plan: MW by type (a dash where the plan could not build that # type), then its cost and the cap's shadow price. No plan builds coal, so it is left out. shown_types = [1, 3, 4, 5, 6] # nuclear, CCGT, CT, wind, solar function plan_row(label, plan) row = "| $(label) |" for g in shown_types if g in plan.types row *= " $(commas(plan.build[g])) |" else row *= " – |" end end return row * " $(commas(plan.cost / 1e6)) | −$(round(-plan.carbon_price; digits=2)) |" end type_columns = "Nuclear (MW) | CCGT (MW) | CT (MW) | Wind (MW) | Solar (MW) | Cost (\\\$M/yr) | Shadow price (\\\$/t) |" println("::: {.small}\n") println("| Plan | ", type_columns) println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|") println(plan_row("Thermal only", capped_thermal)) println(plan_row("All types", capped_all)) println("\n:::") ``` ::: {.small} | Plan | Nuclear (MW) | CCGT (MW) | CT (MW) | Wind (MW) | Solar (MW) | Cost (\$M/yr) | Shadow price (\$/t) | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | Thermal only | 878 | 1,325 | 547 | – | – | 1,095 | −147.91 | | All types | 0 | 1,516 | 737 | 988 | 1,654 | 576 | −14.84 | ::: ::: {.caption} Emission factors $e_g$: coal 1, CCGT 0\.43, CT 0\.55 t/MWh; nuclear, wind and solar 0. ::: The cap is **half** the thermal-only plan's emissions, 3,339 kt of CO~2~ a year: $\sum_{g,t} e_g \, y_{g,t} \leq E$. ::: {.notes} Without a cap the thermal-only plan emits 6,679 thousand tonnes a year. Halving that with thermal types only means building 878 MW of nuclear in place of CCGT, and the plan's cost goes from \$603M to \$1,095M a year. With wind and solar available the same cap costs \$576M, barely more than the uncapped plan with wind and solar (\$570M), because that plan already emitted only 61% of the thermal-only total. Look at the last column: the two shadow prices differ by a factor of ten. ::: ## Why \$148 a Tonne? Swap a MW of CCGT for nuclear, both running all year: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} $$ \frac{\overbrace{(790{,}000 / 8{,}784 + 8)}^{\text{nuclear, \$/MWh}} - \overbrace{(82{,}000 / 8{,}784 + 25)}^{\text{CCGT, \$/MWh}}}{0.43 \text{ t/MWh}} $$ That is **\$147\.9 per tonne**, the thermal-only shadow price. ::: ::: {.fragment .fade-in} This **carbon price** is the cost of abating the last tonne. With wind and solar it is **\$15**. ::: ::: {.notes} Board item; the fragments carry the answer. With thermal types only, the LP reported a shadow price of −\$147\.91 a tonne on the last slide. The shadow price tells a utility what one more tonne of allowed emissions is worth, or what the last tonne of abatement costs. With thermal types only there is one way to abate: replace a CCGT with a nuclear plant, both running all year, and the arithmetic gives the shadow price. With wind and solar there are cheaper ways to avoid a tonne, so the price of the last tonne is far lower. A cap's shadow price depends on what the system is able to build. ::: ## Tightening the Cap ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"} capped_quarter = solve_plan(1:n_all; cap=0.25 * thermal_emissions) capped_tenth = solve_plan(1:n_all; cap=0.1 * thermal_emissions) nuclear_use = capped_tenth.energy[1] / (capped_tenth.build[1] * n_hours) ccgt_use_quarter = capped_quarter.energy[3] / (capped_quarter.build[3] * n_hours) # The tables leave coal out, which is right only if no plan builds it @assert max(with_renewables.build[2], capped_thermal.build[2], capped_all.build[2], capped_quarter.build[2], capped_tenth.build[2]) < 0.5 println("::: {.small}\n") println("| Cap | ", type_columns) println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|") println(plan_row("50%", capped_all)) println(plan_row("25%", capped_quarter)) println(plan_row("10%", capped_tenth)) println("\n:::") ``` ::: {.small} | Cap | Nuclear (MW) | CCGT (MW) | CT (MW) | Wind (MW) | Solar (MW) | Cost (\$M/yr) | Shadow price (\$/t) | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | 50% | 0 | 1,516 | 737 | 988 | 1,654 | 576 | −14.84 | | 25% | 0 | 1,613 | 588 | 2,717 | 2,198 | 672 | −175.85 | | 10% | 629 | 1,190 | 380 | 3,311 | 1,928 | 1,113 | −623.02 | ::: The carbon price rises as the cap tightens. Nuclear is built only at the tightest cap, and produces **38%** of what it could. ::: {.notes} Each cap is a share of the thermal-only plan's emissions. The price rises because the cheapest abatement is used first. At 50% the plan adds wind and solar. At 25% it adds much more, and some of what they could produce goes unused in sunny or windy hours. At 10% nuclear appears. At the 25% cap the price, \$176, is already above the \$148 that nuclear cost on the last slide, yet no nuclear is built. The \$148 assumed a nuclear plant replacing a CCGT that runs all year. With this much wind and solar, the CCGTs produce only 26% of what they could, so a nuclear plant that replaces them avoids far fewer tonnes for the same fixed cost. ::: # Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule ## Key Takeaways ::: {.incremental} - Capacity expansion chooses **what to build** and **how to run it** together, at least total cost. - **Screening curves** read a thermal build off the load duration curve: CT below 1,700 h, unserved below 7\.25 h. - At any finite penalty, some unserved energy is optimal. - The value of wind and solar depends on *when* they produce. - A **CO~2~ cap's shadow price is a carbon price**: \$148/t with thermal types only, \$15/t once wind and solar can be built. ::: ## Next Classes **Wednesday, November 4**: Quiz 4, then mixed integer programming. **Monday, November 9**: Solid waste and network models (with a substitute). **Wednesday, November 11**: Lab 3, fixed costs and facility siting in `JuMP` (with the TA). ## Assessments **Mini-Project 2**: Due Thursday, November 19. Most hours the CCGT or CT is marginal. In the unserved hours the price is the penalty itself. One hour sits in between: it's degenerate (the peaking capacity exactly meets demand), so the shadow price there isn't unique. A CT earns its fixed cost back only in the scarcity hours: 7.25 hours times about 8,965 dollars of margin is about 65,000 dollars, its annual fixed cost. :::
